entries.721af5e58e8872ce0a60f4184a494ef727f1f87b: <div sID="gen18484" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="6" osisID="Ezek.6" sID="Ezek.6"/> <div eID="gen18484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18485" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18486" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. A threatening of the destruction of Israel for their idolatry, and the destruction of their idols with them, <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.1-Ezek.6.7">ver. 1-7</reference>. II. A promise of the gracious return of a remnant of them to God, by true repentance and reformation, <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.8-Ezek.6.10">ver. 8-10</reference>. III. Directions given to the prophet and others, the Lord's servants, to lament both the iniquities and the calamities of Israel, <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.11-Ezek.6.14">ver. 11-14</reference>.
entries.7f6c0b97fd91b6e1d45ef3d643883036bed09a7c: <div eID="gen18486" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18485" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Destruction of Idolatry. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 594.)</title> <div sID="gen18487" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came unto me, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Son of man, set thy face toward the mountains of Israel, and prophesy against them, <hi type="super">3</hi> And say, Ye mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> to the mountains, and to the hills, to the rivers, and to the valleys; Behold, I, <hi type="italic">even</hi> I, will bring a sword upon you, and I will destroy your high places. <hi type="super">4</hi> And your altars shall be desolate, and your images shall be broken: and I will cast down your slain <hi type="italic">men</hi> before your idols. <hi type="super">5</hi> And I will lay the dead carcases of the children of Israel before their idols; and I will scatter your bones round about your altars. <hi type="super">6</hi> In all your dwelling-places the cities shall be laid waste, and the high places shall be desolate; that your altars may be laid waste and made desolate, and your idols may be broken and cease, and your images may be cut down, and your works may be abolished. <hi type="super">7</hi> And the slain shall fall in the midst of you, and ye shall know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen18487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18488" type="x-p"/> Here, I. The prophecy is directed to <hi type="italic">the mountains of Israel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.6.1-Ezek.6.2">v. 1, 2</reference>); the prophet must <hi type="italic">set his face towards</hi> them. If he could see so far off as the land of Israel, <hi type="italic">the mountains</hi> of that land would be first and furthest seen; towards them therefore he must look, and look boldly and stedfastly, as the judge looks at the prisoner, and directs his speech to him, when he passes sentence upon him. Though <hi type="italic">the mountains of Israel</hi> be ever so high and ever so strong, he must <hi type="italic">set his face against</hi> them, as having judgments to denounce that should shake their foundation. <hi type="italic">The mountains of Israel</hi> had been <hi type="italic">holy mountains,</hi> but now that they had polluted them with their high places God set his face against them and therefore the prophet must. Israel is here put, not, as sometimes, for the ten tribes, but for the whole land. <hi type="italic">The mountains</hi> are called upon to <hi type="italic">hear the word of the Lord,</hi> to shame the inhabitants that would not hear. The prophets might as soon gain attention from the <hi type="italic">mountains</hi> as from that <hi type="italic">rebellious and gainsaying people,</hi> to whom they all day long <hi type="italic">stretched out their hands in vain. Hear, O mountains! the Lord's controversy</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mic.6.1-Mic.6.2">Mic. vi. 1, 2</reference>), for God's cause will have a hearing, whether we hear it or no. But from <hi type="italic">the mountains the word of the Lord</hi> echoes <hi type="italic">to the hills, to the rivers, and to the valleys;</hi> for to them also <hi type="italic">the Lord God</hi> speaks, intimating that the whole land is concerned in what is now to be delivered and shall be witnesses against this people that they had fair warning given them of the judgments coming, but they would not take it; nay, they contradicted the message and persecuted the messengers, so that God's prophets might more safely and comfortably speak to <hi type="italic">the hills and mountains</hi> than to them. <div eID="gen18488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18489" type="x-p"/> II. That which is threatened in this prophecy is the utter destruction of the idols and the idolaters, and both by the sword of war. God himself is commander-in-chief of this expedition against <hi type="italic">the mountains of Israel.</hi> It is he that says, <hi type="italic">Behold, I, even I, will bring a sword upon you</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.6.3">v. 3</reference>); the sword of the Chaldeans is at God's command, goes where he sends it, comes where he brings it, and lights as he directs it. In the desolations of that war, <div eID="gen18489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18490" type="x-p"/> 1. The idols and all their appurtenances should be destroyed. The <hi type="italic">high places,</hi> which were on the tops of mountains (<reference osisRef="Ezek.6.3">v. 3</reference>), shall be levelled <hi type="italic">and made desolate</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.6.6">v. 6</reference>); they shall not be beautified, shall not be frequented as they had been. The <hi type="italic">altars,</hi> on which they offered sacrifice and burnt incense to strange gods, <hi type="italic">shall be broken</hi> to pieces and <hi type="italic">laid waste;</hi> the <hi type="italic">images</hi> and <hi type="italic">idols</hi> shall be defaced, <hi type="italic">shall be broken and cease,</hi> and be cut down, and all the fine costly works about them shall be abolished, <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.4">v. 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.6">6</reference>. Observe here, (1.) That war makes woeful desolations, which those persons, places, and things that were esteemed most sacred cannot escape; for <hi type="italic">the sword devours one as well as another.</hi> (2.) That God sometimes ruins idolatries even by the hands of idolaters, for such the Chaldeans themselves were; but, as if the deity were a local thing, the greatest admirers of the gods of their own country were the greatest despisers of the gods of other countries. (3.) It is just with God to make that a desolation which we make an idol of; for he is a jealous God and will not bear a rival. (4.) If men do not, as they ought, destroy idolatry, God will, first or last, find out a way to do it. When Josiah had destroyed the high places, altars, and images, with the sword of justice, they set them up again; but God will now destroy them with the sword of war, and let us see who dares re-establish them. <div eID="gen18490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18491" type="x-p"/> 2. The worshippers of idols and all their adherents should be destroyed likewise. As <hi type="italic">all their high places shall be laid waste,</hi> so shall all <hi type="italic">their dwelling-places</hi> too, even <hi type="italic">all their cities,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.6">v. 6</reference>. Those that profane God's dwelling-place as they had done can expect no other than that he should abandon theirs, <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.11">ch. v. 11</reference>. <hi type="italic">If any man defile the temple of God, him will God destroy,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.17">1 Cor. iii. 17</reference>. It is here threatened that <hi type="italic">their slain shall fall in the midst of them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.6.7">v. 7</reference>); there shall be abundance slain, even in those places which were thought most safe; but it is added as a remarkable circumstance that they shall fall <hi type="italic">before their idols</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.6.4">v. 4</reference>), that their <hi type="italic">dead carcases</hi> should be <hi type="italic">laid,</hi> and their <hi type="italic">bones scattered, about their altars,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.5">v. 5</reference>. (1.) Thus their idols should be polluted, and those places profaned by the dead bodies which they had had in veneration. If they will not <hi type="italic">defile the covering of their graven images,</hi> God will, <reference osisRef="Isa.30.22">Isa. xxx. 22</reference>. The throwing of the carcases among them, as upon the dunghill, intimates that they were but dunghill-deities. (2.) Thus it was intimated that they were but dead things, unfit to be rivals with <hi type="italic">the living God;</hi> for the carcases of dead men, that, like them, <hi type="italic">have eyes and see not, ears and hear not,</hi> were the fittest company for them. (3.) Thus the idols were upbraided with their inability to help their worshippers, and idolaters were upbraided with the folly of trusting in them; for, it should seem, they fell by the sword of the enemy when they were actually before their idols imploring their aid and putting themselves under their protection. Sennacherib was slain by his sons when he was <hi type="italic">worshipping in the house of his god.</hi> (4.) The sin might be read in this circumstance of the punishment; the <hi type="italic">slain men</hi> are <hi type="italic">cast before the idols,</hi> to show that <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> they are slain, because they worshipped those idols; see <reference osisRef="Jer.8.1-Jer.8.2">Jer. viii. 1, 2</reference>. Let the survivors observe it, and take warning not to worship images; let them see it, and know that <hi type="italic">God is the Lord,</hi> that <hi type="italic">the Lord he is God</hi> and he alone.
entries.da9202d9c54de38b1c859328750fc95fe839b854: <div eID="gen18491" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Mercy Promised to the Penitent; Effect of Repentance. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 594.)</title> <div sID="gen18492" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> Yet will I leave a remnant, that ye may have <hi type="italic">some</hi> that shall escape the sword among the nations, when ye shall be scattered through the countries. <hi type="super">9</hi> And they that escape of you shall remember me among the nations whither they shall be carried captives, because I am broken with their whorish heart, which hath departed from me, and with their eyes, which go a whoring after their idols: and they shall loathe themselves for the evils which they have committed in all their abominations. <hi type="super">10</hi> And they shall know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , <hi type="italic">and that</hi> I have not said in vain that I would do this evil unto them. <div eID="gen18492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18493" type="x-p"/> Judgment had hitherto triumphed, but in these verses mercy rejoices against judgment. A sad end is made of this provoking people, but not a full end. The ruin seems to be universal, and <hi type="italic">yet will I leave a remnant,</hi> a little remnant, distinguished from the body of the people, a few of many, such as are left when the rest perish; and it is God that leaves them. This intimates that they deserved to be cut off with the rest, and would have been cut off if God had not left them. See <reference osisRef="Isa.1.9">Isa. i. 9</reference>. And it is God who by his grace works that in them which he has an eye to in sparing them. Now, <div eID="gen18493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18494" type="x-p"/> I. It is a preserved remnant, saved from the ruin which the body of the nation is involved in (<reference osisRef="Ezek.6.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">That you may have some who shall escape the sword.</hi> God said (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.12">ch. v. 12</reference>) that he would <hi type="italic">draw a sword after those</hi> who were <hi type="italic">scattered,</hi> that destruction should pursue them in their dispersion; but here is <hi type="italic">mercy remembered in the midst of</hi> that <hi type="italic">wrath,</hi> and a promise that some of <hi type="italic">the Jews of the dispersion,</hi> as they were afterwards called, should <hi type="italic">escape the sword.</hi> None of those who were to <hi type="italic">fall by the sword about</hi> Jerusalem <hi type="italic">shall escape;</hi> for they trust to Jerusalem's walls for security, and shall be made ashamed of that vain confidence. But some of them <hi type="italic">shall escape the sword among the nations,</hi> where, being deprived of all other stays, they stay themselves upon God only. They are said to <hi type="italic">have</hi> those who shall <hi type="italic">escape;</hi> for they shall be the seed of another generation, out of which Jerusalem shall flourish again. <div eID="gen18494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18495" type="x-p"/> II. It is a penitent remnant (<reference osisRef="Ezek.6.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">Those who escape of you shall remember me.</hi> Note, To those whom god designs for life he will give <hi type="italic">repentance unto life.</hi> They are reprieved, and <hi type="italic">escape the sword,</hi> that they may have time to return to God. Note, God's patience both leaves room for repentance and is an encouragement to sinners to repent. Where God designs grace to repent he allows space to repent; yet many who have the space want the grace, many who <hi type="italic">escape the sword</hi> do not forsake the sin, as it is promised that these shall do. This remnant, here marked for salvation, is a type of the remnant reserved out of the body of mankind to be monuments of mercy, who are made safe in the same way that these were, by being brought to repentance. Now observe here, <div eID="gen18495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18496" type="x-p"/> 1. The occasion of their repentance, and that is a mixture of judgment and mercy-judgment, that they were <hi type="italic">carried captives,</hi> but mercy, that they <hi type="italic">escaped the sword</hi> in the land of their captivity. They were driven out of their own land, but not out of the land of the living, <hi type="italic">not chased out of the world,</hi> as other were and they deserved to be. Note, The consideration of the just rebukes of Providence we are under, and yet of the mercy mixed with them, should engage us to repent, that we may answer God's end in both. And true repentance shall be accepted of God, though we are brought to it by our troubles; nay, sanctified afflictions often prove means of conversion, as to Manasseh. <div eID="gen18496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18497" type="x-p"/> 2. The root and principle of their repentance: <hi type="italic">They shall remember me among the nations.</hi> Those who <hi type="italic">forgot God</hi> in the land of their peace and prosperity, who <hi type="italic">waxed fat and kicked,</hi> were brought to remember him in the land of their captivity. The prodigal son never bethought himself of his father's house till he was ready to perish for hunger in the far country. Their remembering God was the first step they took in returning to him. Note, Then there begins to be some hopes of sinners when they have sinned against the Lord, and to enquire, <hi type="italic">Where is God my Maker?</hi> Sin takes rise in forgetting God, <reference osisRef="Jer.3.21">Jer. iii. 21</reference>. Repentance takes rise from the remembrance of him and of our obligations to him. God says, <hi type="italic">They shall remember me,</hi> that is, "I will give them grace to do so;" for otherwise they would for ever forget him. That grace shall find them out wherever they are, and by bringing God to their mind shall bring them to their right mind. The prodigal, when he remembered his father, remembered how he has <hi type="italic">sinned against Heaven and before</hi> him; so do these penitents. (1.) They remember the base affront they had put upon God by their idolatries, and this is that which an ingenuous repentance fastens upon and most sadly laments. They had departed from God to idols, and given that honour to pretended deities, the creatures of men's fancies and the work of men's hands, which they should have given to the God of Israel. They <hi type="italic">departed from</hi> God, from his word, which they should have made their rule, from his work, which they should have made their business. <hi type="italic">Their hearts departed from</hi> him. The heart, which he requires and insists upon, and without which <hi type="italic">bodily exercise profits nothing,</hi> the <hi type="italic">heart,</hi> which should be set upon him, and carried out towards him, when that <hi type="italic">departs from</hi> him, is as the treacherous elopement of a wife from her husband or the rebellious revolt of a subject from his sovereign. <hi type="italic">Their eyes</hi> also <hi type="italic">go after their idols;</hi> they doted on them, and had great expectations from them. Their hearts followed their eyes in the choice of their gods (they must have gods that they could see), and then their eyes followed their hearts in the adoration of them. Now the malignity of this sin is that it is spiritual whoredom; it is a <hi type="italic">whorish heart</hi> that <hi type="italic">departs from</hi> God; and they are <hi type="italic">eyes</hi> that <hi type="italic">go a whoring after their idols.</hi> Note, Idolatry is spiritual whoredom; it is the breach of a marriage-covenant with God; it is the setting of the affections upon that which is a rival with him, and the indulgence of a base lust, which deceives and defiles the soul, and is a great wrong to God in his honour, (2.) They remember what a grief this was to him and how he resented it. They shall remember <hi type="italic">that I am broken with their whorish heart and their eyes</hi> that are full of this spiritual adultery, not only angry at it, but grieved, as a husband is at the lewdness of a wife whom he dearly loved, grieved to such a degree that he is broken with it; it breaks his heart to think that he should be so disingenuously dealt with; he is broken as an aged father is with the undutiful behaviour of a rebellious and disobedient son, which sinks his spirits and makes him to stoop. <hi type="italic">Forty years long was I grieved with this generation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.95.10">Ps. xcv. 10</reference>. <hi type="italic">God's measures were broken</hi> (so some); a stop was put to the current of his favours towards them, and he was even compelled to punish them. This they shall remember in the day of their repentance, and it shall affect and humble them more than any thing, not so much that their peace was broken, and their country broken, as <hi type="italic">that God was broken</hi> by their sin. Thus <hi type="italic">they shall look on him whom they have pierced and shall mourn,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.12.10">Zech. xii. 10</reference>. Note, Nothing grieves a true penitent so much as to think that his sin has been a grief to God and to the Spirit of his grace. <div eID="gen18497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18498" type="x-p"/> 3. The product and evidence of their repentance: <hi type="italic">They shall loathe themselves for the evils which they have committed in all their abominations.</hi> Thus God will give them grace to qualify them for pardon and deliverance. Though he had been <hi type="italic">broken by their whorish heart,</hi> yet he would not quite cast them off. See <reference osisRef="Isa.57.17-Isa.57.18">Isa. lvii. 17, 18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.2.13-Hos.2.14">Hos. ii. 13, 14</reference>. His goodness takes occasion from their badness to appear the more illustrious. Note, (1.) True penitents see sin to be an abominable thing, that <hi type="italic">abominable thing which the Lord hates</hi> and which makes sinners, and even their services, odious to him, <reference osisRef="Jer.44.4">Jer. xliv. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.1.11">Isa. i. 11</reference>. It defiles the sinner's own conscience, and makes him, unless he be past feeling, an abomination to himself. An idol is particularly called <hi type="italic">an abomination,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.44.19">Isa. xliv. 19</reference>. Those gratifications which the hearts of sinners were set upon as delectable things the hearts of penitents are turned against as detestable things. (2.) There are many <hi type="italic">evils committed in these abominations,</hi> many included in them, attendant on them, and flowing from them, many transgressions in one sin, <reference osisRef="Lev.16.21">Lev. xvi. 21</reference>. In their idolatries they were sometimes guilty of whoredom (as in the worship of Peor), sometimes of murder (as in the worship of Moloch); these were <hi type="italic">evils committed in their abominations.</hi> Or it denotes the great malignity there is in sin; it is an abomination that has abundance of evil in it. (3.) Those that truly loathe sin cannot but loathe themselves because of sin; self-loathing is evermore the companion of true repentance. Penitents quarrel with themselves, and can never be reconciled to themselves till they have some ground to hope that God is reconciled to them; nay, <hi type="italic">then</hi> they shall lie down in their shame, when he is pacified towards them, <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.63">ch. xvi. 63</reference>. <div eID="gen18498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18499" type="x-p"/> 4. The glory that will redound to God by their repentance (<reference osisRef="Ezek.6.10">v. 10</reference>): "<hi type="italic">They shall know that I am the Lord;</hi> they shall be convinced of it by experience, and shall be ready to own it, <hi type="italic">and that I have not said in vain that I would do this evil unto them,</hi> finding that what I have said is made good, and made to work for good, and to answer a good intention, and that it was not without just provocation that they were thus threatened and thus punished." Note, (1.) One way or other God will make sinners to know and own that he is the Lord, either by their repentance or by their ruin. (2.) All true penitents are brought to acknowledge both the equity and the efficacy of the word of God, particularly the threatenings of the word, and to justify God in them and in the accomplishment of them.
entries.72307c240d7714a6efb321e6eb42e728531393f2: <div eID="gen18499" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Prophet's Lamentation. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 594.)</title> <div sID="gen18500" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; Smite with thine hand, and stamp with thy foot, and say, Alas for all the evil abominations of the house of Israel! for they shall fall by the sword, by the famine, and by the pestilence. <hi type="super">12</hi> He that is far off shall die of the pestilence; and he that is near shall fall by the sword; and he that remaineth and is besieged shall die by the famine: thus will I accomplish my fury upon them. <hi type="super">13</hi> Then shall ye know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , when their slain <hi type="italic">men</hi> shall be among their idols round about their altars, upon every high hill, in all the tops of the mountains, and under every green tree, and under every thick oak, the place where they did offer sweet savour to all their idols. <hi type="super">14</hi> So will I stretch out my hand upon them, and make the land desolate, yea, more desolate than the wilderness toward Diblath, in all their habitations: and they shall know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen18500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18501" type="x-p"/> The same threatenings which we had before in the foregoing chapter, and in the former part of this, are here repeated, with a direction to the prophet to lament them, that those he prophesied to might be the more affected with the foresight of them. <div eID="gen18501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18502" type="x-p"/> I. He must by his gestures in preaching express the deep sense he had both of the iniquities and of the calamities of the house of Israel (<reference osisRef="Ezek.6.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">Smite with thy hand and stamp with thy foot.</hi> Thus he must make it to appear that he was in earnest in what he said to them, that he firmly believed it and laid it to heart. Thus he must signify the just displeasure he had conceived at their sins, and the just dread he was under of the judgments coming upon them. Some would reject this use of these gestures, and call them antic and ridiculous; but God bids him use them because they might help to enforce the word upon some and give it the setting on; and those that know the worth of souls will be content to be laughed at by the wits, so they may but edify the weak. Two things the prophet must thus lament:—1. National sins. <hi type="italic">Alas! for all the evil abominations of the house of Israel.</hi> Note, The sins of sinners are the sorrows of God's faithful servants, especially the <hi type="italic">evil abominations of the house of Israel,</hi> whose sins are more abominable and have more evil in them than the sins of others. Alas! <hi type="italic">What will be in the end hereof?</hi> 2. National judgments. To punish them for these abominations <hi type="italic">they shall fall by the sword, by the famine, and by the pestilence.</hi> Note, It is our duty to be affected not only with our own sins and sufferings, but with the sins and sufferings of others; and to look with compassion upon the miseries that wicked people bring upon themselves; as Christ <hi type="italic">beheld Jerusalem and wept over it.</hi> <div eID="gen18502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18503" type="x-p"/> II. He must inculcate what he had said before concerning the destruction that was coming upon them. 1. They shall be run down and ruined by a variety of judgments which shall find them out and follow them wherever they are (<reference osisRef="Ezek.6.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">He that is far off,</hi> and thinks himself out of danger, because out of the reach of the Chaldeans' arrows, shall find himself not out of the reach of God's arrows, which fly day and night (<reference osisRef="Ps.91.5">Ps. xci. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">He shall die of the pestilence. He that is near</hi> a place of strength, which he hopes will be to him a place of safety, <hi type="italic">shall fall by the sword,</hi> before he can retreat. <hi type="italic">He that</hi> is so cautious as not to venture out, but <hi type="italic">remains</hi> in the city, <hi type="italic">shall</hi> there <hi type="italic">die by the famine,</hi> the saddest death of all. <hi type="italic">Thus will</hi> God <hi type="italic">accomplish his fury,</hi> that is, do all that against them which he had purposed to do. 2. They shall read their sin in their punishment; for <hi type="italic">their slain men shall be among their idols, round about their altars,</hi> as was threatened before, <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.5-Ezek.6.7">v. 5-7</reference>. There, where they had prostrated themselves in honour of their idols, God will lay them dead, to their own reproach and the reproach of their idols. They lived among them and shall die among them. They had offered sweet odours to their idols, but there shall their dead carcases send forth an offensive smell, as it were to atone for that misplaced incense. 3. The country shall be all laid waste, as, before, <hi type="italic">the cities</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.6.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will make the land desolate.</hi> That fruitful, pleasant, populous country, that has been as the garden of the Lord, the glory of all lands, shall be <hi type="italic">desolate, more desolate than the wilderness towards Diblath,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.14">v. 14</reference>. It is called Diblathaim (<reference osisRef="Num.33.46">Num. xxxiii. 46</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.48.22">Jer. xlviii. 22</reference>), that <hi type="italic">great and terrible wilderness</hi> which is described, <reference osisRef="Deut.8.15">Deut. viii. 15</reference>, wherein were <hi type="italic">fiery serpents and scorpions.</hi> The land of Canaan is at this day one of the most barren desolate countries in the world. City and country are thus depopulated, <hi type="italic">that the altars may be laid waste and made desolate,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.6">v. 6</reference>. Rather than their idolatrous altars shall be left standing, both town and country shall be laid in ruins. Sin is a desolating thing; therefore <hi type="italic">stand in awe and sin not.</hi>  <chapter eID="Ezek.6"/> <div eID="gen18503" type="x-p"/>

entries.efcdea54a12a67eecaae29b00ed7f654cd65a793: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11034"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 6</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ezek.6.1-Ezek.6.14">Eze 6:1-14</reference>. Continuation of the Same Subject.</title> <div sID="gen19877" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11034"/><hi type="bold">2. mountains of Israel--</hi>that is, of Palestine in general. The mountains are addressed by personification; implying that the Israelites themselves are incurable and unworthy of any more appeals; so the prophet sent to Jeroboam did not deign to address the king, but addressed the altar (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.13.2">1Ki 13:2</reference>). The mountains are specified as being the scene of Jewish idolatries on "the high places" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.6.3">Eze 6:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.26.30">Le 26:30</reference>). <div eID="gen19877" type="x-p"/>
entries.70434726fdb7630090bb2efb1ccf3770f04f08aa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11035"/><div sID="gen19878" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11035"/><hi type="bold">3. rivers--</hi>literally, the "channels" of torrents. Rivers were often the scene and objects of idolatrous worship. <div eID="gen19878" type="x-p"/>
entries.8933946b4e628c619ccb47ec5c2031dfe53c1433: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11036"/><div sID="gen19879" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11036"/><hi type="bold">4. images--</hi>called so from a Hebrew root, "to wax hot," implying the mad ardor of Israel after idolatry [Calvin]. Others translate it, "sun images"; and so in <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.6">Eze 6:6</reference> (see <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.11">2Ki 23:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.4">2Ch 34:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.17.8">Is 17:8</reference>, Margin).<div eID="gen19879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19880" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cast your slain men before your idols--</hi>The foolish objects of their trust in the day of evil should witness their ruin. <div eID="gen19880" type="x-p"/>
entries.159850ce3bd80b6408f086cb5c4dc39b60c2ac2b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11037"/><div sID="gen19881" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11037"/><hi type="bold">5. carcasses ... before ... idols--</hi>polluting thus with the dead bones of you, the worshippers, the idols which seemed to you so sacrosanct. <div eID="gen19881" type="x-p"/>
entries.ff4a2224d208fc43efdc9dde34beabf365f6799f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11038"/><div sID="gen19882" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11038"/><hi type="bold">6. your works--</hi>not gods, as you supposed, but the mere work of men's hands (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.18-Isa.40.20">Is 40:18-20</reference>). <div eID="gen19882" type="x-p"/>
entries.9344e9612e7a4eac28097cd1ca5d3f902c3598f4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11039"/><div sID="gen19883" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11039"/><hi type="bold">7. ye shall know that I am the Lord--</hi>and not your idols, lords. Ye shall know Me as the all-powerful Punisher of sin. <div eID="gen19883" type="x-p"/>
entries.22c475f7cbd3e4c0033929d40850f62640d43846: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11040"/><div sID="gen19884" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11040"/>8. Mitigation of the extreme severity of their punishment; still their life shall be a wretched one, and linked with exile (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.2">Eze 5:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.12">12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.16">12:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.22">14:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.44.28">Jr 44:28</reference>). <div eID="gen19884" type="x-p"/>
entries.68f112a9f95e4c05dd34ca4904d55b032d2118d4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11041"/><div sID="gen19885" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11041"/><hi type="bold">9. they that escape of you shall remember me--</hi>The object of God's chastisements shall at last be effected by working in them true contrition. This partially took place in the complete eradication of idolatry from the Jews ever since the Babylonian captivity. But they have yet to repent of their crowning sin, the crucifixion of Messiah; their full repentance is therefore future, after the ordeal of trials for many centuries, ending with that foretold in <reference osisRef="Zech.10.9">Zec 10:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.13.8">13:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.13.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.14.1-Zech.14.4">14:1-4</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.11">11</reference>. "They shall remember me in far countries" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.16">Eze 7:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.30.1-Deut.30.8">De 30:1-8</reference>).<div eID="gen19885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19886" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I am broken with their whorish heart--</hi>Fairbairn translates, actively, "I will break" their whorish heart; English Version is better. In their exile they shall remember how long I bore with them, but was at last compelled to punish, after I was "broken" (My long-suffering wearied out) by their desperate (<reference osisRef="Num.15.39">Nu 15:39</reference>) spiritual whorishness [Calvin], (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.40">Psa 78:40</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.7.13">Is 7:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.43.24">43:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.10">63:10</reference>).<div eID="gen19886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19887" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">loathe themselves--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Lev.26.39-Lev.26.45">Le 26:39-45</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.42.6">Job 42:6</reference>). They shall not wait for men to condemn them but shall condemn themselves (<reference osisRef="Ezek.20.43">Eze 20:43</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.31">36:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.42.6">Job 42:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.31">1Co 11:31</reference>). <div eID="gen19887" type="x-p"/>
entries.a29170dc07c01ecc3bcc66870ba70732c654607a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11042"/><div sID="gen19888" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11042"/>11. Gesticulations vividly setting before the hearers the greatness of the calamity about to be inflicted. In indignation at the abominations of Israel extend thine hand towards Judea, as if about to "strike," and "stamp," shaking off the dust with thy foot, in token of how God shall "stretch out His hand upon them," and tread them down (<reference osisRef="Ezek.6.14">Eze 6:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.21.14">Eze 21:14</reference>). <div eID="gen19888" type="x-p"/>
entries.76c97ee890425cc2dc689ff5b85240888e9a6ed8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11043"/><div sID="gen19889" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11043"/><hi type="bold">12. He that is far off--</hi>namely, from the foe; those who in a distant exile fear no evil.<div eID="gen19889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19890" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he that remaineth--</hi>he that is left in the city; not carried away into captivity, nor having escaped into the country. Distinct from "he that is near," namely, those outside the city who are within reach of "the sword" of the foe, and so fall by it; not by "famine," as those left in the city. <div eID="gen19890" type="x-p"/>
entries.501ea09295ff475e48979d94c0677b03dc4e7ada: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11044"/><div sID="gen19891" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11044"/><hi type="bold">14. Diblath--</hi>another form of Diblathaim, a city in Moab (<reference osisRef="Num.33.46">Nu 33:46</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.48.22">Jr 48:22</reference>), near which, east and south of the Dead Sea, was the wilderness of Arabia-Deserta. <chapter eID="Ezek.6"/>

entries.53633c6abf289ca860aa62a53c9b016ec2f09506: <div eID="gen31347" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen31348" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31349" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31349" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31348" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31350" type="x-p"/> In this chapter, which forms a distinct section, the prophet denounces the judgments of God against the Jews for their idolatry, <reference osisRef="Eze.6.1-Eze.6.7">Eze 6:1-7</reference>; but tells them that a remnant shall be saved, and brought to a sense of their sins by their severe afflictions, <reference osisRef="Eze.6.8-Eze.6.14">Eze 6:8-14</reference>.
entries.eb404d7c6b8c0cd86db42fbb20da94099dc86da8: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen31350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31351" type="x-p"/> Set thy face toward the mountains of Israel - This is a new prophecy, and was most probably given after the four hundred and thirty days of his lying on his left and right side were accomplished. By Israel here, Judea is simply meant; not the ten tribes, who had long before been carried into captivity. Ezekiel uses this term in reference to the Jews only. <div eID="gen31351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31352" type="x-p"/> The mountains may be addressed here particularly, because it was on them the chief scenes of idolatry were exhibited.
entries.9f14f87c56e4e6cb048bd3be06bf619ec4f50a58: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen31352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31353" type="x-p"/> Your images shall be broken - Literally, your sun images; representations of the sun, which they worshipped. See the margin.
entries.500ff6a4881f87c4709cd746b6d8aa3a74237bf1: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen31353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31354" type="x-p"/> Will scatter your bones round about your altars - This was literally fulfilled by the Chaldeans. According to Baruch, 2:24, 25, they opened the sepulchres of the principal people, and threw the bones about on every side.
entries.82cbf0d4ba759ee3a023d798648aaec66304f12d: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen31354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31355" type="x-p"/> They that escape of you shall remember me - Those that escape the sword, the pestilence, and the famine, and shall be led into captivity, shall plainly see that it is God who has done this, and shall humble themselves on account of their abominations, leave their idolatry, and worship me alone. And this they have done from the Babylonish captivity to the present day.
entries.4e647ed70193dfc9e1e1e53d22e5c580d065c805: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen31355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31356" type="x-p"/> Smite with thine hand, and stamp with thy foot - Show the utmost marks of thy astonishment and indignation, and dread of the evils that are coming upon them. Some have contended for the propriety of clapping and stamping in public worship from these words! It is scarcely a breach of charity to think that such persons are themselves incapable either of attending on or conducting the worship of God. To be consistent, they should copy the prophet in his other typical actions as well as these; and then we shall hear of their lying on their left side for three hundred and ninety days, and on their right side for forty days; shaving their heads, burning their hair, baking their bread with dung, etc. Now all these things, because they were typical and commanded, were proper in the prophet: in such persons as the above they would be evidences of insanity. Such extravagant acts are no part of God's worship.
entries.4994bdd86c0220eddf9f74c8c605315dd6213e4c: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen31356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31357" type="x-p"/> And make the land - more desolate than the wilderness toward Diblath - Diblath or Diblathayim is situated in the land of Moab. It is mentioned <reference osisRef="Num.33.46">Num 33:46</reference>, Almon-Diblathaim; and in <reference osisRef="Jer.48.22">Jer 48:22</reference>, Beth-Diblathaim. It was a part of that horrible wilderness mentioned by Moses, <reference osisRef="Deu.8.15">Deu 8:15</reference>, "wherein were fiery serpents, and scorpions, and drought." The precise reason why it is mentioned here is not very evident. Some think it is the same as Riblah, where Nebuchadnezzar slew the princes of Israel, and put out Zedekiah's eyes; the principal difference lying between the ד daleth and the ר resh, which in MSS. is often scarcely discernible; and hence vast multitudes of various readings. Five, probably six, of Kennicott's MSS. have רבלתה riblathah, as likewise two of my oldest MSS.; though in the margin of one a later hand directs the word to be read בדלת bedaleth, with daleth. But all the Versions read the word with a D. This may appear a matter of little importance, but we should take pains to recover even one lost letter of the word of God.  <chapter eID="Ezek.6"/> <div eID="gen31357" type="x-p"/>

entries.55859b57d37ad3a512ecb9096e40e6266efe06a9: <div eID="gen14824" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">The Judgment upon the Idolatrous Places, and on the Idol-Worshippers</title> <div sID="gen14825" type="x-p"/> To God’s address in <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.5-Ezek.5.17">Eze 5:5-17</reference>, explaining the signs in <reference osisRef="Ezek.4.1-Ezek.4.5">Eze 4:1-5</reference>, are appended in <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.1-Ezek.6.14">Eze 6:1-14</reference> and 7 two additional oracles, which present a further development of the contents of these signs, the judgment portrayed by them in its extent and greatness. In <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.1-Ezek.6.14">Eze 6:1-14</reference> there is announced, in the first section, to the idolatrous places, and on their account to the land, desolation, and to the idolaters, destruction (<reference osisRef="Ezek.6.3-Ezek.6.7">Eze 6:3-7</reference>); and to this is added the prospect of a remnant of the people, who are dispersed among the heathen, coming to be converted to the Lord (<reference osisRef="Ezek.6.8-Ezek.6.10">Eze 6:8-10</reference>). In the second section the necessity and terrible character of the impending judgment is repeatedly described at length as an appendix to <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.12">Eze 6:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.14">Eze 6:14</reference> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.6.11-Ezek.6.14">Eze 6:11-14</reference>). <div eID="gen14825" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">The Desolation of the Land, and Destruction of the Idolaters</title> <div sID="gen14826" type="x-p"/> Eze 6:1. <hi type="italic">And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: </hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.2">Eze 6:2</reference> <hi type="italic">. Son of man, turn thy face towards the mountains of Israel, and prophesy against them.</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.3">Eze 6:3</reference> <hi type="italic">. And say, Ye mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord Jehovah: Thus saith the Lord Jehovah to the mountains, and to the hills, to the valleys, and to the low grounds, Behold, I bring the sword upon you, and destroy your high places.</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.4">Eze 6:4</reference> <hi type="italic">. Your altars shall be made desolate, and your sun-pillars shall be broken; and I shall make your slain fall in the presence of your idols.</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.5">Eze 6:5</reference> <hi type="italic">. And I will lay the corpses of the children of Israel before their idols, and will scatter your bones round about your altars.</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.6">Eze 6:6</reference> <hi type="italic">. In all your dwellings shall the cities be made desolate, and the high places waste; that your altars may be desolate and waste, and your idols broken and destroyed, and your sun-pillars hewn down, and the works of your hands exterminated.</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.7">Eze 6:7</reference> <hi type="italic">. And the slain will fall in your midst; that you may know that I am Jehovah.</hi> - With <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.1">Eze 6:1</reference> cf. Eze 3:16. The prophet is to prophesy against the mountains of Israel. That the mountains are mentioned (<reference osisRef="Ezek.6.2">Eze 6:2</reference>) as <hi type="italic">pars pro toto</hi>, is seen from <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.3">Eze 6:3</reference>, when to the mountains and hills are added also the valleys and low grounds, as the places where idolatry was specially practised; cf. Hos 4:13; <reference osisRef="Jer.2.20">Jer 2:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.6">Jer 3:6</reference>; see on Hos. <hi type="italic">l.c.</hi> and Deu 12:2. אפיקים, in the older writings, denotes the “river channels,” “the beds of the stream;” but Ezekiel uses the word as equivalent to valley, i.e., נחל, a valley with a brook or stream, like the Arabic wady. גּיא, properly “deepening,” “the deep ground,” “the deep valley;” on the form גּאיות, cf. Ewald, §186 <hi type="italic">da</hi>. The juxtaposition of mountains and hills, of valleys and low grounds, occurs again in <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.4">Eze 36:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.6">Eze 36:6</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Ezek.35.8">Eze 35:8</reference>; the opposition between mountains and valleys also, in <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.5-Ezek.32.6">Eze 32:5-6</reference>, and Eze 24:13. The valleys are to be conceived of as furnished with trees and groves, under the shadow of which the worship of Astarte especially was practised; see on v. 15. On the mountains and in the valleys were sanctuaries erected to Baal and Astarte. The announcement of their destruction is appended to the threatening in <reference osisRef="Lev.26.30">Lev 26:30</reference>, which Ezekiel takes up and describes at greater length. Beside the בּמות, the places of sacrifice and worship, and the חמּנים, pillars or statues of Baal, dedicated to him as the sun-god, he names also the altars, which, in Lev. <hi type="italic">l.c. </hi>and other places, are comprehended along with the בּמות eht htiw; see on <reference osisRef="Lev.26.30">Lev 26:30</reference> and 1Ki 3:3. With the destruction of the idol temples, altars, and statues, the idol-worshippers are also to be smitten, so as to fall down in the presence of their idols. The fundamental meaning of the word גּלּוּלים, “idols,” borrowed from Lev. <hi type="italic">l.c.</hi>, and frequently employed by Ezekiel, is uncertain; signifying either “logs of wood,” from גּלל, “to roll” (Gesen.), or <hi type="italic">stercorei</hi>, from גּל, “dung;” not “monuments of stone” (Hävernick). <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.6.5">Eze 6:5</reference></hi> is taken quite literally from <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Lev.26.30">Lev 26:30</reference></hi>. The ignominy of the destruction is heightened by the bones of the slain idolaters being scattered round about the idol altars. In order that the idolatry may be entirely rooted out, the cities throughout the whole land, and all the high places, are to be devastated, Eze 6:6. The forms תּישׁמנה and יאשׁמוּ are probably not to be derived from שׁמם (Ewald, §138 <hi type="italic">b</hi>), but to be referred back to a stem-form ישׁם, with the signification of שׁמם, the existence of which appears certain from the old name ישׁימון in Ps 68 and elsewhere. The א in יאשׁמו is certainly only <hi type="italic">mater lectonis</hi>. In <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.7">Eze 6:7</reference>, the singular חלל stands as indefinitely general. The thought, “slain will fall <hi type="italic">in your midst</hi>,” involves the idea that not all the people will fall, but that there will survive some who are saved, and prepares for what follows. The falling of the slain - the idolaters with their idols - leads to the recognition of Jehovah as the omnipotent God, and to conversion to Him.
entries.8a2fca0b7c2467c22291b9f8ff400bd6087ec309: <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.8-Ezek.6.10">Eze 6:8-10</reference> <div eID="gen14826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14827" type="x-p"/> The survivors shall go away into banishment amongst the heathen, and shall remember the word of the Lord that will have been fulfilled. - Eze 6:8. <hi type="italic">But I shall preserve a remnant, in that there shall be to you some who have escaped the sword among the nations, when he shall be dispersed among the lands.</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.9">Eze 6:9</reference> <hi type="italic">. And those of you who have escaped, will make mention of me among the nations whither they are led captive, when I have broken to me their whorish heart, which had departed from me, and their eyes, which went a whoring after their idols: and they shall loathe themselves because of the evil which they have done in reference to all their abominations.</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.10">Eze 6:10</reference> <hi type="italic">. And ye shall know that I am Jehovah. Not in vain have I spoken this evil to you.</hi> - הותיר, <hi type="italic">superstites facere</hi>, “to make or preserve survivors.” The connection with 'בּהיות וגו is analogous to the construction of הותיר, in the sense of “giving a superabundance,” with בּ <hi type="italic">rei</hi>, <reference osisRef="Deut.28.11">Deu 28:11</reference> and <reference osisRef="Deut.30.9">Deu 30:9</reference>, and is not to be rejected, with Ewald and Hitzig, as inadmissible. For בּהיות is supported by the old versions, and the change of והותרתּי into ודבּרתּי, which would have to be referred to <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.7">Eze 6:7</reference>, is in opposition to the twofold repetition of the וידאתּם כּי אן (וידעוּ), <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.10">Eze 6:10</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.14">Eze 6:14</reference>, as this repetition shows that the thought in <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.7">Eze 6:7</reference> is different from that in 17, 21, not “they shall know that Jehovah has spoken,” but “they shall know that He who has done this is Jehovah, the God of Israel.” The preservation of a remnant will be shown in this, that they shall have some who have escaped the sword. הזּרותיכם is <hi type="italic">infin. Niph</hi>. with a plural form of the suffix, as occurs elsewhere only with the plural ending ות of nouns, while Ezekiel has extended it to the ות of the infinitive of ה''ל verbs; cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.31">Eze 16:31</reference>, and Ewald, §259 <hi type="italic">b</hi>. The remembrance of Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Ezek.6.9">Eze 6:9</reference>) is the commencement of conversion to Him. אשׁר before נשׁבּרתּי is not to be connected as relative pronoun with לבּם, but is a conjunction, though not used conditionally, “if,” as in <reference osisRef="Lev.4.22">Lev 4:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.11.27">Deu 11:27</reference>, and elsewhere, but of time, ὅτε, “when,” as <reference osisRef="Deut.11.6">Deu 11:6</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Chr.35.20">2Ch 35:20</reference>, and נשׁבּרתּי in the signification of the <hi type="italic">futur. exact</hi>. The <hi type="italic">Niphal</hi> נשׁבּר here is not to be taken as passive, but middle, <hi type="italic">sibi frangere</hi>, i.e., לבּם, <hi type="italic">poenitentiâ conterere animum eorum ut ad ipsum</hi> (<hi type="italic">Deum</hi>) <hi type="italic">redeant</hi> (Maurer, Hävernick). Besides the heart, the eyes also are mentioned, which God is to smite, as the external senses which allure the heart to whoredom. ונקטוּ corresponds to וזכרוּ at the beginning of the verse. קוּט, “the later form for קוּץ, “to feel a loathing,” <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi>, “to be filled with loathing;” cf. <reference osisRef="Job.10.1">Job 10:1</reference> with ב <hi type="italic">object</hi>., “in (on) their פנים, faces,” i.e., their persons or themselves: so also in <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.43">Eze 20:43</reference>; Eze 36:31. אל הרעות, in allusion to the evil things; 'לכל־תועב, in reference to all their abominations. This fruit, which is produced by chastisement, namely, that he idolaters are inspired with loathing for themselves, and led to the knowledge of Jehovah, will furnish the proof that God has not spoken in vain.
entries.a85bcf0670d7f268e65290d1b27ce5402124605c: <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.11-Ezek.6.14">Eze 6:11-14</reference> <div eID="gen14827" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">The Punishment Is Just and Well Deserved</title> <div sID="gen14828" type="x-p"/> Eze 6:11. <hi type="italic">Thus saith the Lord Jehovah, Smite with thy hand, and stamp with thy foot, and say, Woe on all the wicked abominations of the house of Israel! that they must perish by sword, hunger, and pestilence.</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.12">Eze 6:12</reference> <hi type="italic">. He that is afar off will die by the pestilence; and he that is near at hand shall fall by the sword; and he who survives and is preserved will die of hunger: and I shall accomplish my wrath upon them.</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.13">Eze 6:13</reference> <hi type="italic">. And ye shall know that I am Jehovah, when your slain lie in the midst of your idols round about your altars, on every high hill, upon all the summits of the mountains, and under every green tree, and under every thick-leaved terebinth, on the places where they brought their pleasant incense to all their idols.</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.14">Eze 6:14</reference> <hi type="italic">. And I will stretch out my hand against them, and make the land waste and desolate more than the wilderness of Diblath, in all their dwellings: so shall ye know that I am Jehovah.</hi> - Through clapping of the hands and stamping of the feet - the gestures which indicate violent excitement - the prophet is to make known to the displeasure of Jehovah at the horrible idolatry of the people, and thereby make manifest that the penal judgment is well deserved. הכּה בכפּך is in <reference osisRef="Ezek.21.19">Eze 21:19</reference> expressed more distinctly by הך כּף אל , “to strike one hand against the other,” i.e., “to clap the hands;” cf. Num 24:10. אח, an exclamation of lamentation, occurring only here and in Eze 21:20. אשׁר, <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.11">Eze 6:11</reference>, is a conjunction, “<hi type="italic">at</hi>.” Their abominations are so wicked, that they must be exterminated on account of them. This is specially mentioned in Eze 6:12. No one will escape the judgment: he who is far removed from its scene as little as he who is close at hand; while he who escapes the pestilence and the sword is to perish of hunger. נצוּר, <hi type="italic">servatus</hi>, preserved, as in Isa 49:6. The signification “besieged” (lxx, Vulgate, Targum, etc.), Hitzig can only maintain by arbitrarily expunging הנּשׁאר as a gloss. On <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.6.12">Eze 6:12</reference></hi>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.13">Eze 5:13</reference>; on 13 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.5">Eze 6:5</reference>; and on 13 <hi type="italic">b</hi>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.3">Eze 6:3</reference>, and Hos 4:13; <reference osisRef="Jer.2.20">Jer 2:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.6">Jer 3:6</reference>; Deu 12:2. 'אל כּל־גב, according to later usage, for על כּל־גב. ריח ניחח, used in the Pentateuch of sacrifices pleasing to God, is here transferred to idol sacrifices; see on <reference osisRef="Lev.1.9">Lev 1:9</reference> and Gen 8:21. On account of the prevalence of idolatry in all parts, God will make the land entirely desolate. The union of שׁממה  serves to strengthen the idea; cf. Eze 33:8., Eze 35:3. The words ממּדבּר דּבלתה are obscure, either “in the wilderness towards Diblath” (even to Diblath), or “more than the wilderness of Diblath” (מן of comparison). There is no doubt that דּבלתה is a <hi type="italic">nom. prop.</hi>; cf. the name of the city דּבלתים in <reference osisRef="Jer.48.22">Jer 48:22</reference>; Num 33:46. The second acceptation of the words is more probable than the first. For, if ממּדבּר is the <hi type="italic">terminus a quo</hi>, and דּבלתה the <hi type="italic">terminus ad quem</hi> of the extent of the land, then must ממּדבּר be punctuated not only as status absolut., but it must also have the article; because a definite wilderness - that, namely, of Arabia - is meant. The omission of the article cannot be justified by reference to <reference osisRef="Ezek.21.3">Eze 21:3</reference> or to <reference osisRef="Ps.75.7">Psa 75:7</reference> (Hitzig, Ewald), because both passages contain general designations of the quarters of the world, with which the article is always omitted. In the next place, no <hi type="italic">Dibla</hi> can be pointed out in the north; and the change of <hi type="italic">Diblatha</hi> into <hi type="italic">Ribla</hi>, already proposed by Jerome, and more recently brought forward again by J. D. Michaelis, has not only against it the authority of all the old versions, but also the circumstance that the <hi type="italic">Ribla</hi> mentioned in 2Ki 23:33 did not form the northern boundary of Palestine, but lay on the other side of it, in the land of <hi type="italic">Hamath</hi>; while the הרבלה, named in Num 34:11, is a place on the eastern boundary to the north of the Sea of Gennesareth, which would, moreover, be inappropriate as a designation of the northern boundary. Finally, the extent of the land from the south to the north is constantly expressed in a different way; cf. Num 23:21 (Num 34:8); <reference osisRef="Josh.13.5">Jos 13:5</reference>; 1Ki 8:65; 2 Kings 14:65; <reference osisRef="Amos.6.14">Amo 6:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.13.5">1Ch 13:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.7.8">2Ch 7:8</reference>; and even by Ezekiel himself (<reference osisRef="Ezek.48.1">Eze 48:1</reference>) לבוא  is named as the boundary on the north. The form דּבלתה is similar to תּמנתה for תּמנה, although the name is hardly to be explained, with Hävernick, as an appellation, after the Arabic <hi type="italic">dibl, calamitas, exitium</hi>. The wilderness of <hi type="italic">Diblah</hi> is unknown. With 'וידעוּ כּי וגו the discourse is rounded off in returning to the beginning of <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.13">Eze 6:13</reference>, while the thoughts in <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.13">Eze 6:13</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.14">Eze 6:14</reference> are only a variation of <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.4">Eze 6:4</reference>-7.  <chapter eID="Ezek.6"/> <div eID="gen14828" type="x-p"/>

entries.99c60e0f7b0d8a40a5d7368ba838c6eccde014d0: <div annotateRef="Bible:Ezek.6.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Ezek.6.1" sID="gen71248" type="section"/> <div sID="gen71249" type="x-p"/>The Prophet now turns himself to the kingdom of Israel, since he had formerly spoken concerning the Jews alone. He says that he was <hi type="italic">divinely sent to the mountains of Israel. </hi>The first question may arise about the time; for the kingdom of Israel had been cut off, and the ten tribes dragged into exile- and the kingdom had come to an end in Ezekiel’s time. The time, therefore, does not seem to accord with the denunciation of the Prophet as to what had happened many years previously. But nothing will appear out of place, if we say that it was partly prophecy and partly doctrine, so that the Israelites might understand why they were driven out of their country, and dispersed among the nations. I say that God’s plans were partly explained to the exiles, that they might know why God had driven them to distant lands: for this punishment would not have been useful had not God convinced them of its cause. But although the kingdom had fallen, it is probable that some of the people were remaining: for the Assyrian did not carry off so many thousand men, and his kingdom would have been burdened by such a multitude. Doubtless he collected the flower of the people, and permitted the commonalty to remain there: for he sent from his own kingdom inhabitants for the deserted soil. But the change was great and ruinous to the king himself, and vexatious to all alike. Although, therefore, the kingdom did not exist any longer — nay, even the name of Israel was almost extinct, because there was no mass of people, and they dwelt in their country like foreigners and guests, yet there was still some portion of them left. Now, we collect from the words of the Prophet that they were obstinate, because they were not induced by either the exile of their brethren, or their own calamity, to leave their own superstitions, and embrace the true and pure worship of God.<div eID="gen71249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen71250" type="x-p"/>Since, therefore, this chastisement did not profit them, hence the Prophet is ordered to preach <hi type="italic">against them</hi> It is ascertained from the first chapter that Ezekiel received this command after the destruction of the kingdom of Israel, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ezek.1.1 Bible:Ezek.1.2">Ezekiel 1:1, 2</reference>) for he said that he was divinely stirred up in the thirtieth year after the jubilee, and in the fifth year of the captivity of Jechoniah or Joachim. It is evident, therefore, that the Prophet spake against the land of Israel after the ten tribes had been dispersed. Hence we may elicit that there were still many people there, because it would have been difficult for the Assyrians to receive all the people, and those who remained alive in the country went on in their own abominations, so that it became necessary for some other judgment to be denounced against them, on which we are about to enter. Now, therefore, this principle is established, that the Prophet so treats the slaughter of the kingdom of Israel, that he predicts as about to come to pass what those left in the country by no means feared; for they were persuaded that. they were free from all dangers. But the Prophet shows that God’s wrath was not yet complete, but that their former calamities were only a prelude, and that heavier woes were at hand, because they had so hardened themselves against the power of God. The prophecy, too, has greater weight when the Prophet addressed the mountains than when his discourse was directed to men. So that Ezekiel is not ordered to exhort the Israelites to penitence, and to threaten them with the punishment which still remained, but he is ordered to turn his discourse <hi type="italic">to hills, and mountains, and valleys</hi> Thus God obliquely signifies, first, that the Israelites were deaf, and then unworthy of the trouble which Ezekiel would spend in teaching them. Thus the Prophet sent to Jeroboam did not design to address him, but turning to the altar —<div eID="gen71250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen71251" type="x-p"/>“O altar, altar,” says he, “thus saith Jehovah, Behold a son shall be born to the family of David, by name Josiah, and he shall slay upon thee the priests of the high places, and shall burn upon thee the bones of the dead.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.13.2">1 Kings 13:2</reference>.)<div eID="gen71251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen71252" type="x-p"/>The king was burning incense on the altar, the prophet does not regard him, but as I have just said, directs his discourse to the altar: that was far more vehement than if he had reproved the king sharply. For that was no common reproof, to pass by the king as if he had been only the shadow of a man, and to admonish the dead altar concerning a future event: so also in this place: <hi type="italic">Son of man, set thy face against the mountains of Israel, and prophesy against them</hi> The Prophet might object that the mountains had no ears, and hence that it was only child’s play. But he understood God’s intention, and so obeyed cheerfully, because he saw the people despised and rejected by God because they were deaf and incurable, and meanwhile he knew that his labor would not be lost although he addressed the mountains. For we know that the earth was created for the use of man, and hence God proposes to us examples of his wrath in brutes, trees, the atmosphere, and the heavens, that we may know that admonitions belonging to us are engraven there, although in every other way God turns away his eyes and his face. This, therefore, is a sign of his wrath, when God shows his judgments on all sides, and yet is silent towards us, because we gather from this that we are unworthy of any trouble for our improvement, and this was doubtless the Prophet’s conclusion.<div eID="gen71252" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Ezek.6.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen71248" osisID="Ezek.6.1" type="section"/>
entries.3014c4453b7e6bf2189c2bf783ca39fba595ba61:
Now a clearer expression follows in the third verse: Thou shalt say, ye mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord. Here an audience is required of the mountains which they could not give, but that has respect to mankind, as I have just said. God, therefore, requires the mountains to listen, so that men may understand that an inanimate thing may be endued with sense, if their stupidity is considered. For at length God enforced his judgments against the mountains of Israel. Although, therefore, they could not hear the Prophet speaking, yet they took up his instruction, because it was efficacious in them, and God at length in reality proved that he had not spoken in vain. The event, therefore, openly made the mountains in some way attentive. Neither could they escape the judgment which had been openly denounced. Now he adds, Thus saith Jehovah to the mountains and the hills Ezekiel now addresses not mountains only, as he had been commanded: hence he seems to exceed the prescribed command, for he had been sent to mountains and hills only, but now he says, hear ye mountains, hear ye hills, hear ye valleys. But we said yesterday that prophets sometimes speak briefly, and sometimes explain more fully what they had uttered but shortly. God, therefore, at the beginning spoke only of mountains, but he doubtless comprehended valleys, and the flowing down of rivers, because the Prophet only explains what he had said in one word: hence he speaks to mountains and hills, and then to the pouring down of waters or torrents Jerome translates it rocks, and the Hebrews call whatever is violent אפיק, aphik, hence when there is any violent course they use this word; and so we may understand in this place either rocks or flowing down of waters or torrents, no matter which. But since he afterwards adds valleys, this explanation is to me probable, that the Prophet indeed understands either torrents or the rushing down of waters. Here we must also remark, that those parts are marked out where the Israelites had erected perverse and adulterous worship: for we know that mountains were filled with superstitions, and so also valleys, though the reason was different: for when they erected their altars on the mountains they thought themselves near God, but when they descended into the valleys, their rites were thus performed in shade and obscurity, and thus they thought themselves in this way hidden as it were in a sanctuary. It is sufficiently known that they exercised their idolatries in the mountains as well as the valleys. This, therefore, is the reason why the Prophet here shows that the whole land of Israel was polluted with defilement. Behold, says he, I bring a sword against you. Hence we infer that when the Prophet addresses the mountains, yet he speaks for the sake of man. For the sword could not injure the mountains: for one stone would break a hundred, nay a thousand swords, and yet remain entire. God, therefore, had threatened the mountains with slaughter in vain, nay, when mention is made of the sword, we know that death is understood: for the cause is put for the effect. Hence God addresses men indirectly, but when he directs his discourse to the mountains he shows that men themselves are deaf, and therefore turns away his face from them, and addresses mute elements and inanimate things: and I will destroy, says he, your lofty things He now explains what I have taught before, that mountains, and hills, and valleys, and descending waters are named, because perverse and impure worship flourished there. For by “lofty things,” the Spirit doubtless intends whatever the Israelites had mixed of their own imaginations to corrupt the worship of God. They properly call altars lofty, because they were erected in high and conspicuous places. But the species is here put for the genus. Meanwhile, God signifies that he so abominates all fictitious worship that he cannot bear the sight of the places. The stones indeed of which the altars were built we know to be harmless: for places are not polluted by idolatry of their own will; for as far as the world was created by God it always retains its own nature, but as far as man is concerned, the places themselves were polluted, and the contagion renders them hateful to God. Hence this is put for the detestation of idolatry. He continues the same sentiment, and first denounces that altars should be laid waste. Now it follows —
Ezekiel 6:4
4. And your altars shall be desolate, and your images shall be broken: and I will cast down your slain men before your idols.
4. Et desolabuntur altaria vestra, et conterentur idola vestra, et cadere faciam
Or, “I will lay prostrate ” — Calvin.
occisos coram idolis vestris.
entries.bc8c4a2f99d043bc40e79c766019dc006b94ea82:
Hence it appears how greatly obedience pleases God, and how true it is that it is better than sacrifices. (1 Samuel 15:22; I Kings 12.) For it is certain that the Israelites extolled their own fictions exorbitantly, as if they were worshipping God correctly In the beginning, indeed, Jeroboam cunningly devised those new rites, that he might alienate the ten tribes from the family of David, and at length the error spread, so that they thought that God approved that impious worship. But we see that God abominates them. We should always hold this principle, that although men think that they obey God when they thrust in their own fictions, yet they produce no other effect than to provoke the wrath of God against them. This vengeance, therefore, had not been taken against altars, unless God had been greatly offended with the impious mixture. Your altars, therefore, shall come to ruin and destruction, and then your idols shall be destroyed. Here some understand the idols of the sun, as the noun is taken from heat, which is afterwards repeated: but this divination seems to be too contracted Hence I do not doubt that the idols are so called on account of the mad love with which the worshippers were seized: for throughout the Prophets they are said to be like adulterers, and our Prophet also uses the same language. Idols therefore may very properly derive their name from heat, because their superstitious worshippers inflame themselves with love, and like adulterers run after harlots, as we shall again see. He afterwards uses another word, when he says, I will lay prostrate your slain before your idols: for they call idols גלולים, gelolim, on account of their foulness, nay even filth. We see then in the first place that the fury with which the Israelites were inflamed is condemned by the Prophet, since they perverted the pure and lawful worship of God: then he reproves their enormity because they willingly remained in filth and defilement. But here also we are taught how mightily God is angry with all superstitions, when he not only cites mankind to his tribunal because they profane true piety, but is angry with external instruments — as stones and wood, and, as it were, involves these instruments of idolatry with their authors. It follows —
Ezekiel 6:5
5. And I will lay the dead carcases of the children of Israel before their idols; and I will scatter your bones round about your altars.
5. Et ponam cadavera filiorum Israel coram idolis vestris, et spargam coram idolis suis:
“The relation is in the third person.” — Calvin.
spargam ossa vestra
“He returns again to the second person ” — Calvin.
In circuitu altarium vestrorum
entries.5038459c2cff91c3e3e3ad2342753880397e9df2:
By these words the Prophet signifies that God’s wrath would be manifest, because he impresses certain marks by which it may be judged that the Israelites had provoked his anger; because they had departed from the pure and genuine order of the law. He says, therefore, I will place the carcases of the sons of Israel before their idols, when the carcases were so mingled with the idols, hence it appeared that God was greatly offended. For we know that it was detestable in all sacrifices that either human bones or carcases should be joined with the victims: so that the religion of the Israelites was openly condemned by this sign, so that unless they had been utterly blind, they would acknowledge all their worship to have been abominable. We understand, therefore, the design of God when he says, that he would cast the carcases of the sons of Israel before their idols: as if he had said, I will defile all your rites which seem to you sacred, and I will make them stink even before the unbelievers. But how? for the altar is polluted by contact with a carcase; but the carcases shall be cast there, that the contagion may spread to the altars. And I will sprinkle, says he, your bones around your altars Lastly, he signifies that he would profane those sacred rites which the Israelites had fabricated for themselves with their carcases: by which he understands that they would be doubly disgraced whilst they defiled by their pollutions what they had thought beautiful. The Prophets constantly proclaimed that these rites were folly and an abomination, but still those who were attached to those superstitions pleased themselves. When, therefore, God’s servants effected nothing by their sacred admonitions, at length a real and actual proof was added, when their altars were polluted, and that, too, with their own defilement. For in this God’s remarkable vengeance appeared, as I have formerly said.
Ezekiel 6:6
6. In all your dwellingplaces the cities shall be laid waste, and the high places shall be desolate; that your altars may be laid waste and made desolate, and your idols may be broken and cease, and your images may be cut down, and your works may be abolished.
6. In omnibus habitationibus vestris urbes desolabuntur:
That is, “in every habitable region they will be deserted.” This word we have illustrated before — Calvin.
et excelsa in vastitatem redigentur, ut vastentur et desolentur
Or,” shall be destroyed and perish.” — Calvin.
altaria vestra, et conterantur, et cessent
Or, “abolished,” the same word for idols which is derived from heat. — Calvin.
idola vestra, et excidantur idola vestra, et deleantur opera vestra.
entries.4be5b3a4300eaa7ec1abd1f3ef84020221f54d76:
In other words, the Prophet signifies that God would take vengeance on the superstitions of the ten tribes in all places; whence it is clear, that no corner was free from corruption. For, while he names all habitations, he means that they had defiled every habitable place. Wheresoever they dwelt they had erected their altars and strange worship, as another Prophet reproves them; according to the number of your cities were your Gods. (Jeremiah 2:28; Jeremiah 11:13.) He addresses the Jews there, but the meaning is the same. Hence the Prophet signifies, that it was not a single part only that was polluted with their idolatries, but their filth was spread abroad through the whole land wherever there were any inhabitants. In all your habitations, therefore, the cities shall be deserted When he threatens destruction and desolation to the cities, he means what I have just said, that those places were corrupted by impious superstitions. He adds, and thy high places shall be destroyed or made desolate. Here he explains himself more clearly, that the cities should be reduced to solitude, because their religion was corrupt, and the inhabitants were given up to their own fictions and idolatries. He adds therefore high places to cities, that he may point out the reason of the cities perishing. He adds, that they may be desolate or reduced to a desert: it is again the word חרב, chereb, and your altars may perish. He confirms the same doctrine, namely, that he was so hostile to the cities of Israel because they were all polluted with profane and strange altars. For, as we have said, God had chosen that land to himself, and so all its cities were dedicated to his glory. This, then, might move us to wonder why he threatened them with destruction; for we might readily answer this by saying his counsel was changed. But the Prophet shows, that although the cities themselves were pleasing to God, yet they were hated by him through the corruptions by which they were polluted. Hence he joins high places to altars. Hence a probable conjecture is elicited, that the Israelites did not sacrifice wherever they had erected high places. They had then their own high places when they worshipped false gods, and also their own altars. And since the worship of God was vitiated in both ways, the Prophet, as I have said, here joins them both.
At length he adds, and your idols shall be broken up and cease, or be abolished. Again he uses that reproachful word which I have said is taken from the stench of dung. (Luke 16:15.) But it signifies that which is highly esteemed among men is abominated by God, especially when it is worshipped. And your idols, says he, shall be cut off. I have said that this word is derived from heat. It means, that the idols were the cause of their madness, since the Israelites were so corrupted with impure love that they deserted God and looked only at the idols: but he compares the zeal with which idolaters are maddened to impure and brutal lust. At length he adds, your works shall be destroyed. Here he uses a general name, and significantly points out the difference between the pure worship of God and all corruptions. There is no need of a long discussion if we desire to know how God is to be worshipped. For he rejects and excludes our works. If, therefore, we do not obtrude our works, but only follow what God demands, our worship will be pure, but if we add anything of our own, it is an abomination. We see, therefore, that useful instruction can be collected from one word, namely, that all worship is perverse and disapproved by God when men bring anything forward of themselves. For by works he does not here understand idols made of either wood, or stone, or brass, or gold, or silver, but it comprehends likewise whatever men have fashioned, and whatever can be ascribed to them, because they have not taken them from the mouth of God and the commands of his law.
Ezekiel 6:7
7. And the slain shall fall in the midst of you, and ye shall know that I am the LORD.
